Seer
SEE-ur
n. (the older Israelite title for a prophet; rendering Hebrew ro'eh and chozeh)
English agent-noun from see — one who sees. It renders two Hebrew words built on the same logic, and the KJV keeps the archaic title because Scripture itself treats it as archaic.

Biblical Definition

A seer is a prophet under his older name, and the Bible pauses in the middle of a narrative to tell us so: “Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer” (1 Samuel 9:9). That parenthesis is one of Scripture's few explicit lexicographical notes, and it teaches two things. First, the offices are one: the man who sees what God shows and the man who speaks what God says are the same man, because seeing is for the sake of saying. Second, the title shifted as the office matured — by the monarchy the emphasis had moved from the receiving to the proclaiming. Samuel himself answers to it plainly: “I am the seer” (1 Samuel 9:19). The chronicler lists three court seers as authors of records: “the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer” (1 Chronicles 29:29), which shows the seer as a documenting historian, not a mystic. And when Amaziah the priest of Bethel wants Amos out of the northern kingdom, he uses the title as a sneer: “O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there” (Amos 7:12) — make your living off your visions somewhere else. The state church has always preferred a prophet it pays.

Webster 1828 Definition

The older Israelite title for a prophet, explained by Scripture itself in 1 Samuel 9:9. Samuel, Gad, and Nathan bore it; it carried the duty of writing records; and Amaziah threw it at Amos as an insult.

expand to see more

SEER, n. [from see.] One who sees; as a seer of visions.

2. A prophet; a person who foresees future events. He that is now called a prophet, was beforetime called a seer. 1 Sam. 9.

3. One who has the gift of discerning what is hidden from ordinary sight.

4. In Scripture usage, the title borne by Samuel, Gad and Heman, denoting the recipient of divine communication.

5. Formerly applied also to the keepers of the royal chronicles, who were prophets in office.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 9:9 — "(Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.)"

1 Samuel 9:19 — "And Samuel answered Saul, and said, I am the seer: go up before me unto the high place; for ye shall eat with me to day, and to morrow I will let thee go, and will tell thee all that is in thine heart."

1 Chronicles 29:29 — "Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer,"

Amos 7:12 — "Also Amaziah said unto Amos, O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there:"

Modern Corruption

The English word has been surrendered to fortune-tellers, psychics, and the occult, so that seer now suggests a crystal ball rather than a man under the word of God — and the biblical office is quietly assimilated to divination.

expand to see more

In modern usage a seer is a clairvoyant, and the drift is not innocent. It puts Samuel in the same category as the witch of Endor, whom Saul consulted precisely because Samuel was dead and God had stopped answering him (1 Samuel 28:6-7). Scripture separates the two absolutely: the seer receives what God chooses to disclose and answers to God for reporting it accurately, while the diviner seeks to extract knowledge from the unseen by technique. Deuteronomy 18:10-14 forbids the whole apparatus of observers of times, enchanters, and consulters with familiar spirits, and then in the same passage promises the true Prophet as the alternative. The office and the occult are not two grades of the same gift; they are opposites, and the shared English word hides it.

The second misuse is inside the church rather than outside it. Where the title is revived for a man said to have unusual spiritual sight, it functions to place his impressions beyond examination — the seer sees what others do not, so who can correct him? Scripture builds the correction into the office. The prophet whose word does not come to pass is to be disregarded and was not sent (Deuteronomy 18:22); the Bereans searched the Scriptures daily to test even Paul (Acts 17:11); and 1 Chronicles 29:29 shows the seers producing written records that could be checked. A man whose sight cannot be tested by the written Word is not a seer in the biblical sense whatever he is called.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ro'eh (participle of ra'ah, to see) and chozeh (participle of chazah, to gaze); both mean one who sees, and 1 Samuel 9:9 glosses them by the later term nabi, prophet.

expand to see more

Hebrew ro'eh (H7200 participle) — one seeing; the archaic title in 1 Samuel 9:9, 11, 18-19, used of Samuel.

Hebrew chozeh (H2374) — a gazer, beholder; the title of Gad (2 Samuel 24:11) and Amos's title in Amos 7:12.

Hebrew nabi (H5030) — prophet, spokesman; the later and dominant title, which 1 Samuel 9:9 says replaced ro'eh.

Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, look, perceive; the ordinary verb of sight, which is why the title is not mystical but plain.

Greek has no exact equivalent title; the Septuagint renders both Hebrew terms by ho blepon (the one seeing) or simply prophetes.

Usage

"“He that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer” — Scripture's own note that the two titles name one office."

"“I am the seer” — Samuel identifies himself plainly, without mystique."

"“O thou seer, go, flee thee away” — the establishment's standing offer to the true prophet: prophesy elsewhere, and eat there."
